items.titel: Prix de l'énergie : les Européens veulent des prix maîtrisés et une action commune, tandis que 7 Français sur 10 ont modifié leur usage de la voiture
items.anriss: Selon la huitième enquête sur le climat de la Banque européenne d'investissement (BEI) , conduite par Ipsos BVA entre le 3 et le 25 août auprès de 23 000 personnes de 16 ans et plus dans les 27 États membres et publiée le 5 novembre, trois …

absaetze.t: Selon la dernière enquête de la Banque européenne d'investissement (BEI), trois Européens sur quatre jugent urgente la transition énergétique, mais la flambée des prix de l'énergie pèse lourdement sur leur pouvoir d'achat. Les Français se montrent encore plus préoccupés que la moyenne européenne.

Selon la huitième enquête sur le climat de la Banque européenne d'investissement (BEI), conduite par Ipsos BVA entre le 3 et le 25 août auprès de 23 000 personnes de 16 ans et plus dans les 27 États membres et publiée le 5 novembre, trois Européens sur quatre jugent la transition énergétique urgente pour leur pays.

Ils voient dans la mise en oeuvre de cette transition énergétique, un moyen de réduire la dépendance de l'Union aux importations de pétrole et de gaz (82 %), l'instauration de prix plus stables ou plus bas (79 %) et un ralentissement du changement climatique (76 %). Une majorité dans chaque État membre attend aussi de cette transition qu'elle contribue à protéger le climat.

"Alors que la transition énergétique bat son plein, l'Europe est en passe de se libérer de sa dépendance aux énergies fossiles" estime la présidente de la BEI, Nadia Calviño, dont l'institution financière a investi près de 168 milliards d’euros en faveur de l’énergie propre dans la dernière décennie. "Dans un contexte géopolitique en pleine mutation, c'est à la fois la bonne chose à faire pour la planète et la décision la plus judicieuse pour nos économies, afin de réduire les coûts énergétiques des entreprises et des ménages".
Le pouvoir d'achat au cœur des préoccupations

La question du pouvoir d'achat est au cœur des préoccupations : 60 % des personnes interrogées estiment que la hausse des prix du gaz, des carburants, du fioul ou de l'électricité a fortement réduit leur pouvoir d'achat au cours des douze derniers mois. Pour faire face, 38 % ont réduit leurs dépenses de santé ou d'alimentation et 34 % ont baissé le chauffage. Surtout, 16% se sont endettés, ont demandé une aide financière ou ont différé une facture d'énergie. Les Européens craignent également qu'une transition trop lente n'entraîne une hausse durable des prix et une dépendance accrue aux énergies importées.

Ils soutiennent toutefois massivement une transition européenne et collective : 87 % souhaitent donner la priorité aux énergies bas carbone, en commençant par le solaire (devant l'éolien). Une majorité (55 %) préfère développer une industrie européenne des technologies propres, même si cela prend plus de temps, plutôt que d'accélérer le déploiement avec des équipements importés. Enfin, 68 % veulent une coopération renforcée entre États membres et 59 % sont favorables à une mise en commun des ressources pour financer les investissements nécessaires.
Quel regard les Français portent-ils sur la transition climatique ?

Cette vaste enquête propose également des fiches détaillées pays par pays. Ainsi, plus de huit Français sur dix (85 %) estiment urgent que leur pays mène à bien la transition énergétique. Une demande supérieure à la moyenne européenne (75 %), qui semble en phase avec la trajectoire engagée, tel que le juge Ambroise Fayolle, vice-président de la BEI. "Grâce à son électricité bas carbone et à l’essor des énergies renouvelables, la France est bien placée pour contribuer à l’autonomie énergétique de l’Europe."

Les bénéfices attendus sont d'abord une moindre dépendance aux importations de pétrole et de gaz (79 %), devant la stabilisation ou la baisse des prix (74 %). Ce classement marque une évolution depuis 2022, lorsque le ralentissement du changement climatique se hissait en tête des priorités en France.

Les Français sont en outre particulièrement sensibles aux conséquences financières du changement climatique et de la crise énergétique. Plus d'une personne interrogée sur trois déclare avoir subi un impact financier lié à des phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes au cours des cinq dernières années, la proportion la plus élevée de l'UE. Entre les cyclones Chido et Garance ayant respectivement frappé Mayotte en décembre 2024 et la Réunion en février 2025, les inondations répétées ou encore les violents incendies qui ont ravagé l'Hexagone durant l'été 2026, ces catastrophes semblent être devenues la norme.

Le 5 novembre 2026, la Commission européenne a octroyé 113 millions d'euros au titre du Fonds de solidarité de l'Union européenne (FSUE) à la France et à la Slovaquie afin de les aider à se relever des conséquences de cyclones dévastateurs et d'inondations qui ont provoqué d'importants dégâts et coûté la vie à de nombreuses personnes.

Depuis sa création en 2002, le Fonds de solidarité de l’Union européenne a apporté plus de 11 milliards d'euros de soutien à la suite de 150 catastrophes, dont 130 catastrophes naturelles et 20 urgences sanitaires, dans 25 États membres, au Royaume-Uni et dans 6 pays en voie d'adhésion.

Les hausses des prix du gaz, des carburants, du fioul ou de l'électricité ont fortement réduit le pouvoir d'achat de 66 % d'entre eux au cours des douze derniers mois : 45 % ont réduit leurs dépenses d'alimentation ou de santé, autant ont baissé le chauffage et 14 % se sont endettés, ont demandé une aide ou ont différé une facture d'énergie. Ces prix ont également modifié les habitudes de déplacement d'une majorité de Français, un tiers d'entre eux ayant limité leurs trajets aux besoins essentiels et un peu plus (41 %) ayant renoncé à un week-end, à des vacances ou à une visite familiale. Plus significatif encore : 31 % roulent désormais plus lentement pour économiser du carburant, la proportion la plus élevée de l'UE.

Pour mener la transition énergétique, 88 % des Français souhaitent donner la priorité aux énergies bas carbone. Le solaire arrive en tête (45 %), suivi de très près par le nucléaire (44 %), nettement au-dessus de la moyenne européenne, tandis que l'éolien recueille 19%. Une majorité privilégie enfin le développement d'une industrie européenne des technologies propres, même si cela prend plus de temps, plutôt qu'un déploiement plus rapide fondé sur des équipements importés.
La France, première bénéficiaire des financements de la BEI

Avec 13 milliards d'euros obtenus en 2025, la France est restée le premier bénéficiaire des financements de la Banque européenne d'investissement devant l'Italie et l'Espagne (hors contribution du fonds de relance).

Ce niveau d'investissement en France reflète des priorités désormais clairement affirmées : la lutte contre le changement climatique, l'innovation technologique, la souveraineté énergétique et industrielle, mais aussi, fait plus marquant, la défense et la sécurité.

Sur ces 13 milliards d'euros injectés dans l'économie française, 10,6 milliards proviennent directement de la BEI et 2,4 milliards du FEI (Fonds européen d'investissement), la branche du groupe dédiée au soutien aux petites et moyennes entreprises et au capital-investissement.

items.titel: [Cartes] Essence, diesel : quel est le prix des carburants dans l'Union européenne ?
items.anriss: Combien dépensent les Espagnols, les Allemands ou les Belges pour faire le plein d'essence ou de diesel à la pompe ? En moyenne, un Européen doit débourser 1,93 euros pour un litre d'essence (sans plomb 95) et 2,15 euros pour un litre de …

absaetze.t: Combien dépensent les Espagnols, les Allemands ou les Belges pour faire le plein d'essence ou de diesel à la pompe ? En moyenne, un Européen doit débourser 1,93 euros pour un litre d'essence (sans plomb 95) et 2,15 euros pour un litre de diesel selon les dernières données de la Commission européenne. Mais cette moyenne cache des disparités parfois importantes entre États membres.
Les prix de l'essence SP95 et du gazole dans chaque pays

Les données publiées par la Commission européenne correspondent à une moyenne nationale pour chaque pays, selon le bulletin publié le 5 novembre 2026 et sur la base de prix relevés au 2 novembre. À cette date, le litre d'essence sans plomb 95 (SP95) dépasse les 2 euros dans huit pays de l'UE : au Danemark (2,50 euros), aux Pays-Bas (2,28 euros), en Finlande (2,21 euros), en France (2,16 euros), en Allemagne (2,13 euros), en Grèce (2,13 euros), au Portugal (2,01 euros) et en Italie (2,00 euros).

Pour le litre du gazole, son prix dépasse désormais les 2 euros dans dix-neuf pays, soit dans plus de deux tiers des États membres. Son plus haut niveau est atteint au Danemark (2,53 euros), aux Pays-Bas (2,47 euros) et en Finlande (2,43 euros).

Les Français doivent débourser en moyenne 2,16 euros pour un litre d'essence (SP95) et 2,37 euros pour un litre de gazole, ce qui place respectivement la France à la quatrième place et à la cinquième place des pays avec les prix les plus élevés de l'UE.

À l'inverse, c'est à Malte que l'essence est la moins chère : 1,34 euro le litre. C'est aussi dans ce pays que le prix du diesel défie toute concurrence dans l'UE : 1,21 euro le litre. Cette situation est le fruit d'une politique de prix fixes lancée par l'État qui absorbe l'inflation via des subventions. Cette politique de prix bas coûte toutefois de plus en plus cher aux finances publiques maltaises. L'archipel affiche, de loin, les tarifs les plus bas. Aucun autre pays ne se situe au-dessous de 1,4 euro pour un litre d'essence ou de 1,8 euro pour un litre de gazole.
Une hausse brutale depuis les attaques contre l'Iran

Depuis le déclenchement de la guerre en Iran le 28 février 2026, la hausse des prix du carburant est brutale. Cette flambée s'explique par les craintes sur l'approvisionnement mondial, les perturbations du trafic dans le détroit d'Ormuz et la tension particulière sur les produits raffinés, notamment le diesel et le kérosène, dont l'Europe dépend en partie du Moyen-Orient.

Avant cela, la première grande phase de hausse visible du XXIe siècle remonte aux années 2005-2008, avec une montée presque continue jusqu'au pic de l’été 2008 : le litre de SP95 est passé d'un peu plus de 1,04 euro début janvier 2005 à environ 1,47 euro début juillet 2008. Cette poussée s'inscrit dans le grand cycle mondial de hausse du pétrole de l'époque, porté par une demande très forte, notamment dans les économies émergentes, alors que la production mondiale stagnait davantage. Après ce pic, la crise financière mondiale a provoqué un retournement brutal, avec une rechute des prix en 2008-2009.

Une deuxième grande séquence haussière est ensuite apparue en 2009-2012, puis une troisième en 2021-2022. Après le creux du début 2009, le SP95 est remonté jusqu'à 1,69 euro au printemps 2012, dans un contexte de reprise économique et de tensions d'offre liées notamment à la guerre civile en Libye et aux sanctions contre l'Iran. Plus récemment, après le point bas exceptionnel du Covid (1,16 euro le litre le 4 mai 2020), les prix ont rebondi avec la reprise post-pandémie en 2021, avant de bondir de nouveau en 2022 avec la guerre en Ukraine et la crise énergétique européenne. Mais l'Agence internationale de l'énergie rappelle que les marchés avaient commencé à se tendre dès 2021, avant l'aggravation provoquée par l'invasion russe.
Les taxes sur les carburants diffèrent selon les pays

Pourquoi ces différences de prix de l'essence et du diesel entre États membres de l'UE existent-elles ? Le prix à la pompe est fixé par chaque distributeur en fonction de quatre paramètres principaux : le coût du pétrole et de son raffinage, le coût de son transport, la marge du distributeur et enfin les taxes nationales. Chaque paramètre influe sur la différence des prix à la pompe entre les distributeurs et entre les pays.
Les carburants sont taxés à deux principaux niveaux :
le droit d'accise : un prélèvement fixe par litre qui n'augmente pas automatiquement avec le prix du pétrole. Certains pays imposent aussi des taxes carbone ou d'autres prélèvements.

la taxe sur la valeur ajoutée (TVA) : elle est calculée sur le prix du carburant une fois les droits d'accise et autres prélèvements éventuels ajoutés. Les automobilistes paient donc de la TVA sur les droits d'accise (un impôt sur l'impôt).
Le droit d'accise

Sur les droits d'accise, l'Union européenne exige que les États membres prélèvent un droit minimum de 0,36 € par litre d'essence sans plomb et de 0,33 € par litre de diesel. Mais la fiscalité appliquée aux carburants comporte des écarts importants selon les États membres, d'après les données de la Commission.

A la date du 2 novembre 2026, les Pays-Bas, la Finlande, le Danemark, la Grèce et la France sont les pays appliquant les droits d'accise les plus élevés sur l'essence. S'agissant de l'accise sur le gazole, le classement est différent. Arrive en tête l'Italie, suivie de la France, la Belgique, du Danemark et des Pays-Bas.

La France applique en 2026 un droit d'accise de 0,69 euro par litre d'essence et de 0,61 euro par litre de gazole. Elle se situe ainsi, parmi les Vingt-Sept, à la cinquième place pour l'essence et à la deuxième pour le diesel. La moyenne de l'UE se situant à 0,51 euro le litre pour l'essence et 0,39 euro le litre pour le gazole.
La TVA

En vertu d'une directive de l'UE, la TVA ne peut pas être inférieure à 15 %. Là encore, le taux diffère entre les pays. La Hongrie applique une TVA de 27 % sur les carburants (le taux est le même sur l'essence et le gazole), quand le Luxembourg applique un taux de 17 %. La moyenne européenne est à 21,4 %. La France à 20 % se situe donc en-dessous.
Quels pays taxent le plus ?

En prenant en compte l'ensemble des taxes - accise, TVA et éventuelles taxes supplémentaires, les pays taxant le plus l'essence au 2 novembre 2026 sont les Pays-Bas, le Danemark, la Finlande, la Grèce et la France. Pour ces cinq pays, les taxes représentent entre 55 % et 49 % du prix total de l'essence.
S'agissant de gazole, arrivent en tête le Danemark, l'Italie, la Belgique, la Finlande et la France. Dans ces États, les taxes représentent entre 41 % et 46 % du prix total du gazole.
Pour les deux types de carburants, la France arrive en cinquième position des pays de l'UE taxant le plus, les taxes représentant 49 % du prix total de l'essence et 42 % du prix total du gazole.
Pourquoi en France le prix du gazole augmente-t-il plus vite que celui de l'essence ?

Le droit d'accise sur l'essence est plus élevé que celui sur le gazole, ce qui explique que, hors période de crise, le sans plomb est légèrement plus cher que le diesel. Mais si depuis le déclenchement de la guerre au Moyen-Orient, le 28 février dernier, le prix du gazole a parfois dépassé celui de l'essence, c'est en raison de la loi de l'offre et de la demande. Quand la demande dépasse l'offre, les prix augmentent. Et le diesel est davantage utilisé que le sans plomb, puisqu'il alimente encore la moitié du parc automobile français. D'après l'Insee, en 2024, la consommation de diesel en France a atteint 28 millions de tonnes, contre 11,1 millions pour l'essence (ce chiffre comprend le sans plomb 95 et 98, y compris le superéthanol E85).

items.titel: California governor commutes sentences of more than 500 people on death row
items.anriss: Gavin Newsom cites state values and flaws in the legal system as he grants largest mass clemency in US history.

absaetze.t: California Governor Gavin Newsom has announced that he will commute the sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, the largest mass clemency in United States history.

The announcement on Thursday effectively clears out California’s death row, although the state has not executed a prisoner for 20 years. Those on death row will instead serve life sentences without the possibility of parole.

“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in an open letter.
Support for the death penalty in the US has largely declined since the 1990s, although it still holds majority backing.

A Pew Research Center poll released in August found that 66 percent of Americans supported the punishment for those convicted of murder. Roughly 73 percent, however, acknowledged there was a risk of executing an innocent person.
Because death penalty cases often involve long and arduous legal appeals, many of those on death row are never executed.
Twenty-three states have banned the practice outright, and others have effectively abandoned it even if the punishment remains on the books.

Still, President Donald Trump, a Republican, has championed the death penalty for serious federal crimes. In April, his administration pledged to expand the use of federal executions, including by employing firing squads.
While proponents of the death penalty have argued that the punishment has a deterrent effect, critics say decades of scholarship indicate otherwise.
They have also pointed to ethical and logistical issues, including the expense.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPIC), California has spent $6bn on the death penalty since 1978 while carrying out just 13 executions in that time.
Capital punishment has also been criticised for being applied disproportionately to racial minorities and for the frequency of botched executions.
The DPIC says that, since 1973, at least 203 people wrongly convicted and sentenced to death in the US have later been exonerated.
Newsom’s decision has been praised by criminal justice groups as a step away from a practice they say is outdated, inefficient and immoral.

“Governor Newsom’s announcement marks a decisive moment in the history of the death penalty in the United States. Though other governors have granted universal clemencies, none have been at this scale,” Robin Maher, the executive director of the DPIC, said in a statement.
“By bookending his time as governor first with a moratorium and now this mass clemency, Governor Newsom has irrevocably changed California’s relationship with the death penalty.”

The DPIC noted that about two-thirds of the commutations must be reviewed by the California Supreme Court, which is required under state law to review clemency for anyone with multiple felony convictions, before they become final.

Despite its left-leaning reputation, California previously served as a laboratory for punitive criminal justice policies in the late 20th century, during the heyday of the US’s tough-on-crime politics.
The states of Washington and California, for instance, were among the first to pass “three strikes” laws in the early 1990s, punishing repeat offenders with high minimum sentences.
The state continues to have the largest death row in the country.
Newsom’s decision will reduce the number of people on death row nationally by nearly 30 percent.
The announcement also comes days after a blockbuster night for the Democratic Party in the US midterm elections, with major wins in formerly right-wing strongholds such as Texas and Kansas.
The so-called “blue wave” during the midterms has set off speculation over potential Democratic candidates for the presidency in 2028.
As governor for nearly eight years, Newsom has reached California’s term limits: His second and final term will end in January 2027.
He will be replaced by former US Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra on January 4.
But Newsom has long been seen as a likely presidential contender, and he has increasingly dedicated time to serving as a proxy to support Democratic candidates in key races nationwide.
He has, however, taken positions on criminal justice issues that have put him at odds with criminal justice groups and the state legislature.
In 2022, Newsom vetoed a bill that would have placed limits in state prisons on the use of solitary confinement, a practice defined as torture by the United Nations after certain lengths of time.
In 2019, he also vetoed a measure that would have limited cooperation between Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and prison authorities, and a similar bill failed in the state Senate in 2022.

items.titel: Bundestag korrigiert Panne bei Tabaksteuererhöhung
items.anriss: Eigentlich sollte die Tabaksteuer erst zum Jahreswechsel erhöht werden - doch durch ein Versehen trat die Erhöhung schon jetzt in Kraft. Nun heißt es per Gesetzesänderung: Kommando zurück.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Eigentlich sollte die Tabaksteuer erst zum Jahreswechsel erhöht werden - doch durch ein Versehen trat die Erhöhung schon jetzt in Kraft. Nun heißt es per Gesetzesänderung: Kommando zurück.

Der Bundestag hat einen Fehler bei der Tabaksteuererhöhung nachträglich behoben. Das Parlament stimmte am Donnerstagabend für eine Gesetzesänderung, mit der ein fälschlicherweise zu frühes Inkrafttreten der Steuererhöhung rückgängig gemacht werden soll. Bundestag und Bundesrat hatten Mitte Oktober eine Erhöhung der Tabaksteuer beschlossen. Diese soll nach dem Willen der Regierung ab Anfang 2027 schrittweise ansteigen.

Durch die Steuererhöhung sollen verschiedene Tabakprodukte teurer werden. So steigt etwa der Preis für eine 20er-Packung Zigaretten von derzeit gut 8 Euro bis zum Jahr 2030 in mehreren Schritten auf knapp 12 Euro.
Bundesrat muss noch zustimmen

Eigentlich sollte der erste Erhöhungsschritt am 1. Januar erfolgen. Durch eine fehlerhafte Formulierung im Gesetzestext galt der höhere Steuersatz aber bereits ab seiner Veröffentlichung am 20. Oktober.

Das Bundesfinanzministerium betonte zwar bei Bekanntwerden des Fehler, dass dieser keine tatsächlichen Auswirkungen auf die Steuerzahlungen habe, wollte ihn aber trotzdem rückwirkend korrigieren. Dies geschah nun. Dem Gesetz und damit auch der Korrektur bei der Tabaksteuer muss noch der Bundesrat zustimmen.

items.titel: Turkiye’s parliament ratifies Mecca defence agreement
items.anriss: Parliament's approval lays the groundwork for further Turkish involvement in Saudi Arabia's conflict with the Houthis.

absaetze.t: Parliament’s approval lays the groundwork for further Turkish involvement in Saudi Arabia’s conflict with the Houthis.

Turkiye’s parliament has ratified a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that includes a collective defence clause, committing NATO’s second-largest military to the group’s aid in case of attack.
The ratification on Thursday comes as Riyadh continues to face attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.
Turkiye first signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August and sent it to parliament for ratification last month.
Article 1 of a bill approving the pact was adopted by the Turkish parliament on Wednesday.
But afterwards, Deputy Parliament Speaker Celal Adan adjourned the session until Thursday afternoon, the Anadolu news agency reported.
After parliament returned to session, lawmakers continued to debate the other articles in the pact.
The agreement ultimately passed with 279 votes in favour and 119 against, with 398 of the chamber’s 592 lawmakers taking part in the vote.
The pact contains 16 articles, according to a document submitted to the Turkish parliament, seen by the Reuters news agency.

In Article 1 of the accord, the signatories shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity. Article 1 can be invoked in case of an attack on any member state.
Once the first article is invoked, the document lays out provisions for what follows.

“In the event one of the parties is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the parties shall immediately provide assistance to the party under attack, utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them,” says Article 2 of the pact.

This key clause mirrors Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, the document that established the NATO military alliance. NATO’s Article 5 establishes that an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

Given that Turkiye is a member of both NATO and the Mecca pact, critics have raised questions about whether the country’s government might face a conflict of interest in allocating its military resources.
Turkish officials, however, have dismissed such concerns as unfounded.
Other articles in the Mecca pact concern a mutual agreement to increase defence industry cooperation and military coordination, with the aim of deterring threats.
Those articles, in part, commit member states to conducting joint training, pursuing technological innovation and sharing logistics and intelligence resources.
The draft approved by Turkish lawmakers commits member countries to the pact for 10 years, after which point they may withdraw.
It also leaves open the possibility of other countries joining, with the approval of the pact’s existing members. Syria’s government has already expressed interest.
Despite Thursday’s parliamentary ratification, it is not a foregone conclusion that Turkish troops would be deployed to Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks.
Experts say any Turkish troop deployment would also require other legislative processes.
Turkiye’s Defence Minister Yasar Guler said in October that the scope of potential support for Saudi Arabia would be determined after ratification.
“We absolutely do not foresee entering into any conflict with the Houthis,” Turkish media reported Guler as saying. Instead, Turkish support “would be to strengthen deterrence”.

Tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen had abated somewhat following a 2022 ceasefire. But the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent months, notably launching a series of deadly strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
The region also remains embroiled in the US-Israel war on Iran, which has contributed to cross-border tensions.

On Thursday, Saudi Arabia announced it had intercepted a drone in the region of Medina. Riyadh has accused the Houthis several times of targeting Mecca and Medina, two holy cities in Islam, an accusation the Iran-backed group systematically rejects.

items.titel: Kalifornien wandelt Todesstrafen in lebenslange Haftstrafen um
items.anriss: In Kalifornien wird die Todesstrafe seit 20 Jahren nicht mehr vollstreckt. 548 Menschen sitzen dort aktuell im Todestrakt. Jetzt kündigte der scheidende Gouverneur Newsom an, ihre Strafen in lebenslange Haftstrafen umzuwandeln.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Kaliforniens Gouverneur Todesstrafen werden zu lebenslangen Haftstrafen

In Kalifornien wird die Todesstrafe seit 20 Jahren nicht mehr vollstreckt. 548 Menschen sitzen dort aktuell im Todestrakt. Jetzt kündigte der scheidende Gouverneur Newsom an, ihre Strafen in lebenslange Haftstrafen umzuwandeln.
In Kalifornien sollen Hunderte Todesurteile, die dort noch ausstehen, in lebenslange Haftstrafen umgewandelt werden. Das teilte der scheidende Gouverneur Gavin Newsom mit.

Er werde die Strafen der aktuell 548 Häftlinge im Todestrakt in Kalifornien in lebenslange Haftstrafen ohne die Möglichkeit einer vorzeitigen Entlassung umwandeln, so Newsom in einem Schreiben, das an "alle Kalifornier" gerichtet ist. "Ich ergreife diese Maßnahme, weil ich der festen Überzeugung bin, dass eine vom Staat genehmigte Tötung mit den Werten Kaliforniens nicht vereinbar ist", heißt es weiter.
Ein Schritt gegen Trump

In Kalifornien gibt es die meisten Häftlinge im Todestrakt in den USA. Doch der Bundesstaat vollstreckt die Todesstrafe bereits seit 20 Jahren nicht mehr, der Schritt gilt deshalb als symbolisch. 2019 hatte Newsom ein Moratorium gegen Hinrichtungen in dem Bundesstaat verhängt.

Die Entscheidung Newsoms gilt auch als politisches Signal an Präsident Donald Trump, der ein Verfechter der Todesstrafe ist. Newsom wird seit Längerem als Präsidentschaftskandidat der US-Demokraten gehandelt. Nach zwei Amtszeiten durfte er nicht erneut für den Gouverneursposten kandidieren.
Immer wieder Debatte über Todesstrafe

Die Debatte über die Todesstrafe in den USA hatte nach der gescheiterten Hinrichtung der Todeskandidatin Christa Pike wieder an Fahrt aufgenommen. Die 50-Jährige hatte Ende September in Nashville im Bundesstaat Tennessee zwei Giftspritzen überlebt. Pike war 1995 wegen Mordes an einer Klassenkameradin zum Tode verurteilt worden.

Verteidigungsminister Pete Hegseth sorgte im Oktober mit einer Ankündigung für Empörung, die Exekution des Attentäters Nidal Hasan durch ein Erschießungskommando im Dezember live zu übertragen. Nach massiver öffentlicher Empörung sagte Trump die Liveübertragung allerdings ab.

items.titel: USMC Says It Needs Nine More Amphibious Warships To Carry Out Its Missions
items.anriss: Navy and Marine Corps leaders have recently come to the agreement that the Corps needs 40 amphibious ships to meet its goal of keeping three Marine Expeditionary Units (MEU) deployed at the same time. However, at the moment, the Navy has …

absaetze.t: Navy and Marine Corps leaders have recently come to the agreement that the Corps needs 40 amphibious ships to meet its goal of keeping three Marine Expeditionary Units (MEU) deployed at the same time. However, at the moment, the Navy has only 31 of these vessels, a minimum mandated by Congress, and now an effort is underway to convince lawmakers to increase the fleet.

MEUs, made up of about 2,200 Marines, are typically embarked on Amphibious Ready Groups (ARGs), which usually consist of an assault ship, two transport docks or dock landing ships. Support vessels, surface combatants and in some cases a nuclear fast attack submarine can make up the larger Expeditionary Strike Group.

Marine Corps Commandant Gen. Eric Smith’s top priority is meeting what is called the 3.0 ARG/MEU presence, said Shon Brodie, director of Maritime Expeditionary Warfare at the Corps’ Combat Development and Integration (CD&I) Directorate tasked with modernizing the Marines.

Smith “believes that the best thing that we as a service can do for the nation is provide the highly trained Marine Expeditionary Units, one from the East Coast, one from the West Coast, and that one in Japan, persistently,” Brodie told a small group of reporters, including from TWZ, on Wednesday.

To ensure that happens, Vice Chief of Naval Operations (VCNO) Adm. James W. Kilby and the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps (ACMC) Gen. Bradford J. Gering “have worked really close together to try to understand the number of ships it would require to achieve 3.0 based on current readiness,” Brodie noted.
“The two analytical arms of both services have come to the conclusion that it takes 40 ships. That’s 13 big decks and 27 LPDs,” the Maritime Expeditionary Warfare director explained.

Big decks are the Navy’s Wasp class (LHD) and America class (LHA) amphibious assault ships. Their embarked Aviation Combat Elements (ACEs) can include F-35B Joint Strike Fighters, MV-22 tiltrotor aircraft, UH-1, AH-1 and CH-53 helicopters, as well as Navy Seahawk helicopters. The LPDs are smaller [Amphibious Transport Dock ships], which also embark MV-22s and helicopters.

The capabilities of MEUs have grown over the past decade, allowing them, in limited cases, to take on tasks that once required an aircraft carrier strike group. MV-22 tiltrotors, and, more recently, F-35Bs, which can be embarked in large numbers in the so-called “Lightning carrier” configuration, have boosted the utility of these fighting units.

The amphibious ship requirements, which had been in discussion for a while, were finally hammered out over the past few months by the new Amphibious Force Readiness Board (AFRB), stated Brodie. The AFRB is a joint Navy-Marine Corps effort created to better track the readiness of the amphibious fleet, which has been a huge issue as we have frequently noted.
“Right now, I have 31 amphibious warfare ships,” stated Brodie. The biggest need at the moment, he added, is for additional amphibious assault ships.
The law calls for the service to have 10, but currently it has only nine. That’s because the USS Bonhomme Richard (LHD-6) was sent to the scrapyard in 2021 after being ravaged by a fire in 2020.
Brodie said the Marines want to increase the number of mandated amphibious assault ships from 10 to 13.
“When I have a problem generating this force, it really revolves around the big deck,” he stated.

The call for a fleet of 40 amphibious ships, and especially 13 big decks, is a sharp departure from the guidance former Commandant Gen. David Berger introduced in 2019 that led to his Force Design 2030 plan. In these documents, Berger called for fewer amphibious assault ships and more smaller vessels. Berger was concerned about the growing array of threats to these large, slow-moving vessels from anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles, and that was before one-way attack drones became such ubiquitous weapons of war. This strategy was seen as better suited for fighting in the Pacific in a modern context, not large scale beach landings of the past.

He also wanted to return the Corps to its naval roots; small, dispersed stand-in forces working inside an adversary’s weapons engagement zone after two decades of ground pounding in Afghanistan and Iraq.
Given how much of a sea-change this new plan represents, reaching a 40 amphibious ship fleet that includes 13 big decks is no small task.

“I’ve got a sheet sitting right here in front of me that tells me how we get there,” Brodie added. “You can’t get there tomorrow, right? The only way for me to realistically increase that inventory is for me to build new ships and do a service-life extension on some of the selective ships that I currently have in the inventory.”
Brodie said that Kilby and Gering are going to approach Congress later this month to convey the need for more ships.
There is no set timeline to reach the 40-ship goal, the Marines told TWZ.

“We will have to await future congressional funding for these,” Lt. Col. Eric D. Flanagan, a USMC spokesman, told us, adding that there is a multi-ship procurement contract underway for several amphibious vessels. He was referring to HII being awarded a $9.6 billion multi-ship procurement contract in 2024 for the construction of three San Antonio class amphibious ships and a contract modification for the next America class large-deck amphibious ship.
“This combined procurement — the first of its kind for amphibious ships — begins the journey for the construction of LPDs 33, 34, 35 and LHA 10 for the U.S. Navy,” HII stated at the time.
The request for additional shipbuilding funds will likely face far stiffer headwinds now that the Democrats have won control of both the Senate and the House.

While the Trump administration continues to pursue a roughly $1.5 trillion defense budget for Fiscal Year 2027, which includes some $350 billion that would come from outside normal defense spending streams via the reconciliation process, a letter leaked yesterday from a top Democrat offers a glimpse into the challenges the new amphibious ship plan may face.

The letter from Rep. Adam Smith, a Washington state Democrat who is in line to become chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, makes clear that many programs and policy issues, as well as defense spending writ large, are set to be put under the microscope when the Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

“We must thoroughly review our national defense strategy and develop a more realistic and sustainable approach that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or paid for through draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Smith wrote in his ‘dear colleagues’ letter.

All of this comes at a time when the Navy has been struggling to meet operational demands for surface combatants with its existing fleet. This has been further exacerbated by shakeups in separate plans to acquire new frigates and larger uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), as well as rising costs associated with its workhorse Arleigh Burke class destroyers.
On top of everything, conflicts in the Middle East have taken a toll on the Navy, incurring costs that need to be paid for.

In August, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle estimated as a result of the Operation Epic Fury fight against Iran, the Navy needed between $6 billion and $8 billion more than what was budgeted for in the 2026 fiscal year “to be whole and solvent for [Fiscal Year] 26,” Navy Times reported.

Overall, the U.S. military “has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July,” according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters last month.

In addition to not having enough ships to fulfill the mission, there is a big problem keeping the existing ones available. The Navy’s amphibious ship fleet had just a 47% combat surge readiness rate as of April, according to Kilby’s Fiscal Year 2027 budget request statement. As we have pointed out previously, chronic maintenance delays, competing budget priorities, ill-planned early-retirement efforts that went forward without required congressional approval, scarce spare parts, shoddy contractor oversight and other issues have contributed to these problems.

The Navy and Marines are working to change that and meet the requirements set out by the commandant, Brodie stated. This has involved getting a better handle on how long and how often ships need to be deployed and improving maintenance once underway.

“We’re at the very beginning stage of that, but the indications are, and the models tell us, that we will actually be able to shrink the days in maintenance and improve force generation by some percentage that will be helpful,” Brodie explained. “Without getting into numbers that are probably sensitive, but we’re marginally better than we were before, and the expectation is that we can increase beyond marginally better here over the next couple of maintenance cycles.”

“There’s another factor here that sort of you can’t model in your framework, and that’s extended deployment,” Brodie added. “You’ve got to bring the ship back on time, get it in maintenance on time. If you extend the deployments — and you’ll find that’s true with the whole Navy fleet — if you extend the deployment, and you miss a maintenance cycle, it sort of blows that forecast that you had.”
The problems created by extended deployments are something TWZ frequently highlights.

When regular maintenance doesn’t happen, it creates a cascading series of problems that affect not just the ships and crews, but the facilities that have scheduled repairs and lined up workers to make them happen.

The bottom line is that the longer these vessels stay out on cruise, the longer they have to stay in on deep maintenance, and past a certain point, the magnitude of this relationship skyrockets. Extra days out can turn into extra weeks in the yard, and so on. With yard facilities at a premium, especially those capable of dealing with a supercarrier and big deck amphibious vessels, critical schedules can quickly implode, with work stacking up across multiple vessels, resulting in them being sidelined much longer than planned. This is something we have discussed in great detail when it comes to aircraft carriers.

While the Marines and Navy say they need 40 amphibious ships, whether they reach that level is still an open question that will have to be addressed in future budget cycles. There are a lot of competing needs and only so much money that can be allocated.

items.titel: Shield AI to acquire radar maker Echodyne to bust drones
items.anriss: Shield AI agreed to acquire Echodyne in a $5.3 billion transaction announced Thursday — a major financial transaction that expands the prime defense contractors’ drone-warfare capabilities.

absaetze.t: Shield AI agreed to acquire Echodyne in a $5.3 billion transaction announced Thursday — a major financial transaction that expands the prime defense contractors’ drone-warfare capabilities.

Echodyne produces next-generation, solid-state radar systems patented as Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array (MESA) technology. Its highly advanced systems are flexible and can be easily incorporated into a wide variety of weapons and monitoring systems to detect drones, including high-energy lasers and microwave weapons.

In September, Echodyne was awarded a $250 million contract by the Defense Department’s premier national counter-drone task force, JIATF-401, to provide counter-drone technology to military forces over 36 months.

Speaking to Defense News in July, Echodyne CEO Eben Frankenberg said demand for counter-drone detecting radar is “red hot” and could grow tenfold by 2030. The company produces technology that can track small quadcopter drones and even over 1,000 objects at a time.

“There is a rush of interest globally for counter-drone,” Frankenberg told Defense News. “The Ukraine war made it obvious to everyone that drones had changed the face of warfare, but the Iran war made it obvious that everything’s at risk.”

The acquisition is a bold new move for Shield AI, which is already well-known as the maker of the X-Bat and V-Bat vertical takeoff and landing systems, or VTOL drones. The V-Bat became famous for assisting the U.S. Coast Guard in conducting reconnaissance on illicit drug trafficking at sea and enabling law enforcement to make large maritime drug busts.

The company also builds Hivemind autonomy software, which delivers AI pilots to perform multi-agent teaming and swarming across a wide range of unmanned systems, including unmanned aircraft systems, drone boats and spacecraft.
Shield AI CEO Gary Steele said the purchase of Echodyne supports the company’s aim to branch into three different areas of unmanned systems.

“We are building a new-generation defense technology company consisting of three fast-growing, high-margin, mutually supporting business units: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems,” Steele said in a statement.
Frankenberg said in a statement that Shield AI’s mission complements that of Echodyne and that he expects unity of effort to multiply what both companies can deliver.
“Hundreds of customers rely on our radars to detect and track drones, protect people and infrastructure, secure borders, and ensure safe airspace operations,” Frankenberg said.

“Shield shares our view that autonomous systems can only act on what they can sense, and superior sensors lead to superior systems and outcomes,” he continued. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government, and commercial customers around the globe.”

items.titel: US-Israel relations and Donald Trump’s Middle East policy face uncertainty after Democrat midterm gains
items.anriss: No nation had more at stake in the US midterm elections on Tuesday than Israel and, by extension, the Palestinian territories in Gaza and the West Bank. What was framed as a once-in-a-generation opportunity for Democrats to regain control …

absaetze.t: Politics
November 6, 2026
3 Min Read
The US midterms have coloured the country’s political climate blue. How will this affect the president’s support for Israel?

No nation had more at stake in the US midterm elections on Tuesday than Israel and, by extension, the Palestinian territories in Gaza and the West Bank. What was framed as a once-in-a-generation opportunity for Democrats to regain control of Congress simultaneously became a referendum on America’s historic relationship with the Jewish nation. And no matter who ultimately forms a government after Israel’s inconclusive elections last week, the results of the US midterms will affect the Middle Eastern country’s own fraught and war-weary electorate.

The most consequential midterm race for Israel, if not the entire Middle East, was in Michigan. There, Abdul el-Sayed – an Egyptian-American physician, former Rhodes Scholar and Columbia University assistant professor who led a series of major public health departments – became the state’s next Democrat senator and the first Muslim senator in US history. His win helped to secure the party’s hopes of regaining Congress. But the success of El-Sayed, who battled endless accusations of antisemitism and Islamic fundamentalism during the race, will likely call into question the ideological alignment between Washington and Israel, with clear implications for the presidential race in two years’ time.

Former vice-president and unsuccessful 2024 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris has teased a 2028 run, highlighting Donald Trump’s failure to moderate Israel’s conduct in Gaza. And former president Barack Obama has also been ratcheting up his critiques of Israel as he took to helping Democratic candidates nationwide. Late last month in Michigan, for example, he rallied alongside El-Sayed a few weeks after Harris.

On Tuesday, Trump announced that he had made a deal with Benjamin Netanyahu to reduce annual funding to Israel. Netanyahu, it appears, was well aware of possible international sanctions, having suggested on 25 October that the country might need to use cryptocurrency to bypass them. His comment might have been pre-election hyperbole but the nation nevertheless seems poised to withstand the rescinding of such a seismic and symbolic economic input: its economy is surging, particularly across the tech and investment sectors.

It is more difficult to predict how Trump will go about exacting his plans in the region following this week’s Democratic sweep. The election results will undoubtedly influence how long the president can continue his war in Iran, which he has suggested will resume after the elections. At the same time, he is trying to regain steam for his faltering Board of Peace, recently hiring a former Biden official to help secure bipartisan support for his delayed Gaza reconstruction plan. For now, we can at least expect far stronger pressure on whoever becomes Israel’s next leader to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank, thanks, in large part, to a US in the throes of change.
David Kaufman is a contributing writer at Monocle. For further reactions to the US elections, tune in to Monocle Radio. For more opinion, analysis and insight, subscribe to Monocle today.

items.titel: It’s Time to Talk About Classism in the Art World
items.anriss: For something that determines so much — about the art we make, the art we get to see or not, the art that may never be made at all — the issue of class is rarely discussed in the art world. Breaking the silence, artist and writer Mark …

absaetze.t: In his memoiristic new book, photographer Mark Alice Durant weaves his personal experiences into a larger rebuke of the economic inequality that governs the art world.
November 5, 2026 — 3 min read

For something that determines so much — about the art we make, the art we get to see or not, the art that may never be made at all — the issue of class is rarely discussed in the art world. Breaking the silence, artist and writer Mark Alice Durant speaks up in his memoir-cum-rebuke, Confessions of a Working Class Artist (2026). It reads both like a Künstlerroman and an updated version of the seminal guide for the aspiring artist, Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet (1929), for our dystopian neo-Gilded Age.

For Durant, also the author of the moving photographic memoir Summer of the White Fox, and After (2024) and publisher at Saint Lucy Books, which released both titles, choosing to become an artist was an act of self-exile. He writes that he psychically uprooted himself from the working-class precincts of Boston where he grew up as well as from his extended family, with the exception of his mother, unusually open-minded and supportive of her son. Perhaps she saw herself in his youthful gift of a framed reproduction of Jules Breton’s 1884 painting of a field worker, “The Song of the Lark.” After deciding on this path, Durant writes, “I could never return home on some level.”

items.titel: Ex-husband of Brent Sikkema sentenced to life in prison over murder-for-hire killing
items.anriss: Daniel Sikkema, who was married to Brent Sikkema for 15 years, had been convicted of orchestrating his grisly 2024 murder

absaetze.t: The former husband of the late New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, Daniel Sikkema, aged 56, has been sentenced to life imprisonment for organising Sikkema’s murder in 2024. A federal court in Manhattan handed down the sentence on Wednesday (4 November).

In May 2026, after a two-week trial, Daniel Sikkema was convicted on charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country. In addition to life imprisonment, he was sentenced to five years of supervised release.

Brent Sikkema, who was aged 75 at the time of his murder, was found stabbed to death at his home in the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on 15 January 2024. According to prosecutors, Daniel Sikkema began planning the murder in 2023 in the midst of his divorce from the dealer, with whom he had been married for around 15 years and shared a son.

As the couple’s divorce proceedings became more acrimonious, Daniel Sikkema, who holds dual US and Cuban citizenship, recruited the Cuban national, Alejandro Triana Prevez, as the hitman. On the night of the murder, Prevez entered the late Sikkema’s residence and stabbed him 18 times. Prevez subsequently received $5,000 from Daniel Sikkema and was promised further payments.

Prosecutors said Daniel Sikkema made 11 payments to Prevez and Prevez’s partner in Cuba, using the identities of unwitting friends, employees and family members to conceal the transactions. Prevez was arrested by Brazilian authorities four days after the murder at a gas station on the side of the highway in the state of Minas Gerais, around 600 miles from Rio de Janeiro. He had stolen cash and jewellery in his possession. His case is being handled separately by a Brazilian court.

Brent Sikkema was born in 1948 in Morrison, Illinois, and studied at the San Francisco Art Institute before beginning his career. In the early 1990s, he founded Wooster Gardens in SoHo, moving the gallery to Chelsea in 1999. The business became Sikkema Jenkins & Co in 2003 following the involvement of Michael Jenkins and Meg Malloy.

The gallery is now known as Sikkema Malloy Jenkins and continues to operate in Chelsea. It has championed the work of artists including Kara Walker, Vik Muniz, Sheila Hicks, Jeffrey Gibson and Arturo Herrera. A representative for Sikkema Malloy Jenkins told The Art Newspaper that the gallery will not be providing any statement regarding the conviction or sentencing.

items.titel: SWA implements modular "toolkit" for a more walkable Houston
items.anriss: Landscape architecture studio SWA has designed a modular system including petal-shaped shade structures, outdoor lighting and planting beds that can be deployed around the city in an effort to create a more comfortable streetscape in …

absaetze.t: Landscape architecture studio SWA has designed a modular system including petal-shaped shade structures, outdoor lighting and planting beds that can be deployed around the city in an effort to create a more comfortable streetscape in Houston, Texas, USA.
The Cool & Connected Corridors project seeks to retrofit the streets of Houston with cooling infrastructure to create a more walkable pedestrian experience.
The project is part of the city’s wider Public Realm Action Plan initiative aimed at making the urban streetscape “more delightful, comfortable and easy”, according to the city.

The network of architectural elements is designed to be integrated into varying, pre-existing sidewalk conditions, according to the team, and have been installed along a 15-block stretch of the city’s Texas Avenue as Phase 1 of the Public Realm Action Plan roll-out.

“Cool & Connected Corridors is a blueprint for taking action here and now, showing how cities can layer social, economic, and environmental benefits in a cost-efficient way,” said SWA principal Natalia Beard.

The “easily replicable toolkit” includes three main components – a lighting system aimed at improving visibility and safety at night, modular planting beds and mesh cooling pavilions designed by architecture studio Höweler + Yoon.
The petal-shaped pavilions are made of bead-blasted stainless steel, with mesh membranes in gradients of blue, green and purple.
They stretch up overhead, providing shade on street corners during the day, and integrated lighting illuminates them at night.
According to the team, they were designed to be installed as a single unit, or clustered together to form “bouquets”.
“Together, they create a sequence of shaded landmarks that help orient pedestrians from block to block,” said Höweler + Yoon co-founder Meejin Yoon.
The integrated lighting designed for the system is globe- and line-form lighting that drops down from the tree canopy.
According to the team, it was informed by a lighting study performed by the city in 2023, which identified a master plan for illuminating the nightime streetscape.
Other elements in the Cool & Connected Corridors system include wayfinding, replacement trees and a careful selection of drought-tolerant and pollinator-supportive plants throughout the planters.
The system along Texas Avenue was installed in the city ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

Since its installation, “thermal infrared readings of ground surfaces beneath the shade structures show an average temperature reduction of 10°F (5°C), with reductions of up to 30°F (16°C) in some locations”, said SWA.
Next, the city plans to install the system along the remaining portion of Texas Avenue and along other strips of the downtown area including McKinney Street and Preston Street.
Another recent urbanism project aimed at improving walkability is the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street in London.
Elsewhere in Houston, STG recently released renders of a twisting skyscraper, while the city is also set to receive projects by OMA and Theaster Gates.
